tldr: By using a visual world model (based on TD-MPC2) that integrates wrist-mounted depth images and proprioception, the authors achieved a generalizable insertion policy with a 56% zero-shot success rate on parts with unseen geometries.
hero_caption: Overall view of the InsertionWM system. A single latent world model is trained on 90 diverse part pairs in a GPU-parallelized simulator, achieving high-precision insertion on unseen test parts with no additional training (zero-shot).
overview:
Robotic insertion (mating) tasks in factory assembly lines demand millimeter-level precision. At the same time, part geometries vary immensely, making automation extremely difficult. Prior reinforcement learning approaches predominantly trained dedicated, individual policies (specialists) for each part. However, this required massive retraining and retuning whenever a new part was introduced, lacking practical scalability.

To address this, the authors hypothesized that model-based reinforcement learning (world models) is the key to generalizable insertion policies across diverse geometries. By leveraging dense self-supervised learning signals from environment transition predictions, they reasoned that the model could prevent visual feature interference across multiple tasks while perceiving unseen shapes on the fly from visual feedback to plan actions.

To validate this, they built a proposed framework called "InsertionWM" and trained a latent world model combining raw depth images from a wrist-mounted camera with proprioception such as end-effector pose. Training was conducted on 90 geometrically diverse part pairs, and zero-shot insertion performance was evaluated on 10 completely unseen parts.

As a result, while conventional model-free reinforcement learning (AutoMate) managed only a 7% success rate on unseen parts, InsertionWM achieved a staggering 56% zero-shot success rate. Furthermore, the experiments demonstrated scaling properties where generalization to unseen parts improves as more training parts are added, as well as efficient finetuning capabilities on unseen parts.
contributions: Demonstrating that visual world models dramatically outperform model-free reinforcement learning in multi-task learning and geometric generalization for robotic assembly tasks.
Achieving a 56% zero-shot insertion success rate on unseen part geometries using only raw wrist depth camera images and proprioception, without privileged information such as CAD models.
Showing a clear scaling law where zero-shot success rates on unseen parts improve as the number of trained part categories increases.
Demonstrating that finetuning the generalist world model on novel parts achieves significantly higher sample efficiency and asymptotic performance compared to training from scratch.

sections.heading: Why use "world models" for part insertion now?
sections.summary: Prior robotic assembly research relied on training separate policies per part, making deployment to high-mix low-volume production difficult. This paper demonstrates that introducing predictive world models yields generalizable insertion controllers capable of adapting to unseen shapes directly from raw visual observations.
sections.details:
Robotic assembly in manufacturing is a crucial task requiring extremely high precision. Current industrial solutions rely on hand-crafted controllers, but these break down with even minor shifts in part geometry or placement.

Recent reinforcement learning research has also predominantly followed a "specialist" approach, spending tens of millions of steps training individual policies for each part pair. When attempting to unify these into a single generalist model, model-free reinforcement learning methods like policy gradients struggle with inter-task interference and poor sample efficiency, failing to balance dexterity and generalization.

Here, the authors turned their attention to visual world models. A world model predicts environment dynamics: what the next state and reward will be given the current state and action. Because dense predictive error signals are obtained in a self-supervised manner across all transitions, it can efficiently learn shared visual encoder representations compared to model-free methods that rely solely on sparse success rewards. Furthermore, during inference, it performs local planning (trajectory optimization) in latent space, enabling flexible adaptation to unseen geometries.

The proposed framework, InsertionWM, takes raw depth images from a wrist-mounted camera and proprioceptive information as input. Without using any privileged information such as CAD models, it achieves up to a 56% zero-shot insertion success rate on parts with unseen geometries. Rather than inventing a completely new algorithm, the paper's core argument is that it unlocks the immense latent potential of model-based reinforcement learning for industrial assembly.

sections.heading: The intersection of robotic assembly and model-based RL
sections.summary: Most prior work on simulation-based assembly learning (like AutoMate) relied on low-dimensional states or specialist policies. This work represents the first full-scale application of model-based RL methods like TD-MPC2—which have succeeded in high-precision continuous control—to robotic assembly tasks.
sections.details:
### Prior Work: Learning Robotic Assembly
Robotic insertion tasks have long been challenging due to complex geometries, asymmetry, and tight clearances. In recent years, advances in GPU-parallel simulators have driven progress in training with reinforcement learning in simulation and transferring to real robots (Sim-to-Real). A prominent example is AutoMate, which provided a benchmark of 100 part pairs, training specialists via PPO and exploring generalist policies through distillation using CAD point clouds. However, these methods relied on low-dimensional pose estimates or required CAD models even at test time.

### Positioning of This Work: Introducing Model-Based RL
While reinforcement learning has achieved notable success in tabletop manipulation and legged locomotion, those tasks are relatively forgiving in terms of precision. For inserting unseen parts requiring millimeter-level precision, the authors adopted TD-MPC2, a powerful model-based reinforcement learning algorithm, as their foundation. TD-MPC2 performs local trajectory optimization in latent space and exhibits strong performance on continuous control benchmarks. This research is the first to systematically apply model-based RL to robotic assembly and demonstrate zero-shot generalization directly from raw images.

sections.heading: Problem formulation and algorithm foundations: Reviewing TD-MPC2
sections.summary: The task is formulated as a POMDP, learning latent representations from wrist depth images and proprioception. TD-MPC2 integrates latent dynamics, a value function, and a policy prior to plan optimal actions via MPPI.
sections.details:
### Problem Formulation (POMDP)
Robotic assembly is modeled as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP). Because fully capturing the underlying state is impossible in the real world, observations consist of raw depth images $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{96 \times 96}$ from a wrist camera and robot proprioception $\mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^{24}$. The action $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^6$ is a 6-DoF delta pose command for the end-effector (normalized to $[-1, 1]$).

### Architecture of TD-MPC2
TD-MPC2 avoids decoding observations back to raw images, operating entirely in a latent state $\mathbf{z}$ necessary for control and prediction. The model consists of five neural networks:
- Encoder $h(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{q})$: Maps observations to a latent state $\mathbf{z}$
- Latent dynamics $d(\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{a})$: Predicts the next latent state given an action
- Reward predictor $R(\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{a})$: Predicts immediate rewards
- Value function $Q(\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{a})$: Estimates future returns
- Policy prior $\pi(\mathbf{z})$: Generates candidate actions for sampling-based planning

### Learning and Planning
During training, the model minimizes an end-to-end loss combining latent state prediction, reward prediction, and temporal difference (TD) error across a temporal horizon $H$. During inference (control), it uses the learned dynamics and value functions, initialized with the policy prior, to execute Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control—a sampling-based trajectory optimization algorithm—planning the action sequence with the highest expected return in real time.

sections.heading: Training environment: 100 diverse parts and the Isaac simulator
sections.summary: Using 100 geometrically diverse part pairs from AutoMate, 90 are assigned for training and 10 for unseen testing under a strict split. A Franka Panda robot is trained using wrist depth camera images and noisy proprioceptive inputs.
sections.details:
### Assembly Dataset
The experiments use the 100 part pairs established in the prior AutoMate benchmark. As shown in Figure F2, the set includes not only cylinders but also highly diverse shapes such as asymmetric geometries and gear-like components. Because insertion strategies depend heavily on part shape, a policy capable of recognizing geometry is essential. To eliminate human selection bias, the authors strictly held out the last 10 parts by ID for testing (unseen) and allocated the remaining 90 for training.

### Simulation Setup, Observations, and Rewards
Inside an Isaac Gym environment, a Franka Panda arm with a parallel-jaw gripper is set up, initializing sockets and plugs in randomized poses.
- **Observations**: Alongside a $96 \times 96$ depth image simulating an Intel RealSense D435 on the wrist, proprioception includes 24 dimensions: joint positions (7D), end-effector and socket 6D poses injected with white noise to mimic real-world sensor errors ($2 \times 7$D), and target position (3D).
- **Reward Function**: Adopting AutoMate's reward design directly, it is a linear combination of a mesh penetration penalty $r_{\textnormal{penetration}}$, a distance reward to the target pose $r_{\textnormal{dist}}$, an imitation reward $r_{\textnormal{imitation}}$ based on demonstrations automatically generated by reversing disassembly motions, and a task completion reward $r_{\textnormal{success}}$.
- **Curriculum Learning**: To aid learning, a curriculum automatically adjusts the initial state difficulty (initial distance from the socket) based on the current success rate.

captions.F2: Overview of the 100 part pairs (assemblies) used in the experiments. The 90 pairs enclosed in the top box are used for training, while the 10 in the red box below are held out for unseen test evaluations. Geometric asymmetry and clearance tolerances vary widely across parts.

sections.heading: InsertionWM: Perceiving and inserting unseen geometries
sections.summary: A multimodal encoder fuses wrist depth observations and proprioception. Without using object IDs or CAD models, parallel simulation across 90 environments allows the policy to infer geometry purely from vision, achieving zero-shot generalization.
sections.details:
### Multimodal Observation Encoder
While a single-part specialist can manage with proprioception alone, a generalist handling unseen parts requires "eyes" to directly perceive geometry. InsertionWM employs an encoder $h$ consisting of three modules:
- A shallow convolutional neural network (ConvNet) for depth images: $h_{\textnormal{depth}}$
- A 2-layer MLP for proprioception: $h_{\textnormal{prop}}$
- A 2-layer MLP fusing both representations to output latent state $\mathbf{z}$: $h_{\textnormal{fuse}}$
Each module applies SimNorm normalization to stabilize training.

### Zero-Shot Generalization via Vision
Providing object IDs (such as one-hot vectors) during multi-task training can improve performance on seen parts, but it prevents deployment to unseen parts. Instead, InsertionWM provides no object IDs or CAD models, forcing the model to infer geometric properties autonomously using only the visual cues of the plug and socket visible from the wrist camera (Figure F4).

During training, leveraging GPU parallelism, each of the 90 parts is assigned to separate parallel environment instances for simultaneous data collection. This prevents bias toward specific parts while ensuring robustness against diverse initial poses.

captions.F3: The InsertionWM system pipeline. Depth images from the wrist camera and robot proprioception are fused via an encoder into a latent space, and online planning with the learned world model executes zero-shot insertion on unseen parts.
captions.F4: Example raw depth images captured by the wrist camera. The relative pose and cross-sectional profiles of the grasped plug and the socket below are clearly visible, enabling the model to distinguish geometric differences end-to-end.

sections.heading: Experimental results: 56% zero-shot success and strong scaling laws
sections.summary: On single tasks, specialists achieved a 79.78% success rate (+9.5% over the baseline). In multi-task settings, a single world model trained on 90 parts hit a 56% zero-shot success rate on 10 unseen parts, showing clear performance scaling as training parts increased.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup and Baselines
The model has only 5M parameters. It is compared against state-of-the-art AutoMate (model-free RL using PPO). While an AutoMate specialist trains for 50M steps without vision, an InsertionWM specialist requires only 2M steps (about 40 hours on an RTX 3090). The 90-part generalist also trains highly efficiently in 7M steps (3 days on the same GPU).

### Specialist (Single-Task) Performance
Evaluating individual policies across all 100 parts (Figure F5), InsertionWM achieved an average success rate of 79.78%, significantly outperforming AutoMate's 70.31%. Vision provided notable gains especially on thin, small sockets. However, performance dropped on certain parts where large plugs occluded the socket (e.g., IDs 296, 726).

### Generalist (Multi-Task) and Zero-Shot Generalization
Investigating scaling behavior as training parts increased yielded dramatic results. On seen parts, AutoMate dropped to 15.6% across 80 parts, whereas InsertionWM maintained 55.0% across 90 parts. Crucially, on zero-shot evaluations across 10 unseen parts, AutoMate achieved only ~7%, while InsertionWM reached up to 56%. Success on unseen tasks scaled steadily upward as more parts were added to training, validating the strong scalability of world models.

### Finetuning on Unseen Parts
Finetuning the 90-part pretrained generalist on the 10 unseen parts (Figure F6) demonstrated vastly superior sample efficiency compared to training from scratch. On parts 1036 and 1041, finetuning even surpassed the asymptotic performance of scratch models trained for 2M steps.

### Key Ablation Insights
- **Impact of Vision**: Removing the camera (proprioception only) severely degraded performance, confirming raw visual input is essential for geometric generalization.
- **Camera Placement**: Testing an alternative camera pose with a clearer view of the grasped plug increased occlusions and degraded performance.
- **Curriculum Learning**: Introducing an adaptive curriculum consistently improved performance across tasks.

captions.F5: Evaluation of single-part specialists. Compared to AutoMate (gray: 70.31%), the proposed method (blue: 79.78%) wins on most parts. It struggles on select large parts that cause severe visual occlusion.
captions.F6: Finetuning curves on the 10 unseen parts. Compared to training from scratch (blue lines: solid is early, dashed is at 2M steps), finetuning the pretrained generalist (red lines) reaches high success rates in significantly fewer steps.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future challenges: Hurdles for real-world deployment
sections.summary: This work demonstrates for the first time that data-driven zero-shot insertion into unseen part geometries is achievable using visual world models. Resolving camera occlusion and Sim-to-Real transfer remain the primary research challenges ahead.
sections.details:
This paper demonstrated InsertionWM, an insertion world model that generalizes to unseen geometries by scaling the diversity of training parts. It represents an impactful milestone showing how model-based RL can bring a paradigm shift to manufacturing assembly.

At the same time, the authors outline clear limitations and hurdles for real-world application:
- **Visual Occlusion**: Success rates drop sharply when parts are large or positioned such that the insertion area is occluded by the gripper or wrist.
- **Dataset Scarcity**: Building simulation-ready, high-precision assembly meshes requires extensive manual effort, limiting the current dataset to around 100 parts.
- **Sim-to-Real Transfer Challenges**: Because raw depth images are used instead of low-dimensional pose estimates, bridging the gap with low-cost depth camera noise, blurred edges, and simulated-vs-real contact dynamics remains a substantial hurdle.

The authors highlight active perception—moving the viewpoint to reduce geometric uncertainty before committing to an insertion—as a promising future direction.

takeaways: Even in contact-rich assembly tasks requiring millimeter-level precision, visual latent world models (TD-MPC2) can balance high generalization with dexterity.
While model-free RL suffers from task interference in multi-task insertion, world models scale smoothly thanks to dense, self-supervised transition prediction signals.
Using raw depth images without CAD models or object IDs allows the policy to perceive geometry on the fly, unlocking zero-shot adaptation to unseen parts.
A world model pretrained on a diverse part dataset serves as an exceptionally strong foundation model (initialization) for finetuning on novel parts.
limitations: All evaluations are conducted strictly in simulation (Isaac Gym); real-world sensor noise and contact friction gaps (Sim-to-Real) remain untested.
Relying on a single fixed wrist camera makes the system susceptible to visual occlusions when larger parts block the view of the socket.
The available assembly simulation dataset is limited to around 100 parts, meaning large-scale validation to the point of model capacity saturation has not yet been achieved.
